---
title: "Brighton and Hove's authority effect"
subtitle: "Why the city's schools sit so far above what Value Added v2.1 expects, what explains it, and what might."
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "site_helpers.R"))
V <- load_va()
B <- readRDS(here::here("data", "bh_effect.rds"))
LA <- B$la
t_at <- function(s, col) B$tests[[col]][B$tests$spec == s]
g_at <- function(g, col) B$groups[[col]][B$groups$group == g]
c_at <- function(a, col) B$comp[[col]][B$comp$area == a]
pc <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
yrs <- va_years(V) |> filter(group == "all") |>
  inner_join(V$schools |> select(URN, LANAME), by = "URN")
by_year <- yrs |> filter(LANAME == LA) |> group_by(year_label, provisional) |>
  summarise(va = mean(va), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
gap <- function(col) c_at(LA, col) - c_at("England", col)
# Value added with no allowance for absence (the model without absence), by
# authority, all pupils: authorities with three or more schools
m2 <- readRDS(here::here("data", "place_absence.rds"))$va_m2 |> filter(group == "all") |>
  inner_join(V$schools |> select(URN, LANAME), by = "URN") |>
  group_by(LANAME) |> summarise(va = mean(va_m2), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 3) |> mutate(rank = rank(-va))
m2_la <- m2 |> filter(LANAME == LA)
# The single latest year, mean of schools: the measure the area pages'
# add-and-take figure uses
wl <- va_wide(V)
abs_yr <- yl(max(wl$latest_year))
lat_la <- mean(wl$absence[wl$LANAME == LA], na.rm = TRUE)
lat_eng <- mean(wl$absence, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## In short

On the v2.1 model `r LA` has the `r ord(t_at("v2", "rank"))` largest local
authority effect of `r t_at("v2", "n_la")`: its schools' Attainment 8 runs
`r pc(t_at("v2", "effect"))` above what intake and context predict, after
neighbourhood education is taken into account. **Almost all of it is an
absence effect.** The city's absence is among the highest in England, the
model expects that absence to cost attainment, and in `r LA` it costs much
less than expected. Take absence out of the model and the authority falls
to `r ord(t_at("no_absence", "rank"))`. The extra absence is mostly
authorised illness. Why it costs so little here is the open question, and
family-level resources are one of the likely answers.
:::

# How large, and how steady

The effect is there for every group of pupils and in every year:

```{r tbl-groups}
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0(LA, "'s authority effect on the v2.1 model, by group. The effect on Attainment 8 and its rank among authorities (1 = most above expectation), with and without the absence term.")
B$groups |> transmute(Group = GROUP_LABELS[group],
                      `v2.1 effect` = pc(effect), `v2.1 rank` = paste(rank, "of", n_la),
                      `Without absence` = pc(effect_no_abs), `Rank without absence` = paste(rank_no_abs, "of", n_la)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

```{r fig-bh-years}
#| fig-cap: !expr paste0("Mean value added of ", LA, "'s schools by year, all pupils, Attainment 8 points against England. ", yl(max(by_year$year_label)), " is provisional (hollow).")
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(by_year, aes(year_label, va, group = 1)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_line(colour = DPURPLE, linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = provisional), colour = DPURPLE, fill = "white", size = 2.6, stroke = 1.1) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 16, `TRUE` = 21), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = yl) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Value added (points)") + theme_note()
```

A school in `r LA` averages `r sgn(min(by_year$va))` to
`r sgn(max(by_year$va))` points a year above similar schools in England.
That is not one good cohort.

# It is an absence effect

The test is to refit the model one term at a time. Each row below is the
all-pupils model with one change, on the
`r format(B$rows, big.mark = ",")` school-years that have published
absence reasons:

```{r tbl-tests}
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0(LA, "'s authority effect, all pupils, as the v2.1 model changes. AIC compares fit (lower is better; the published model is the reference). The last column is how closely every authority's effect matches the published model's.")
B$tests |> transmute(Model = label, Effect = pc(effect), Rank = paste(rank, "of", n_la),
                     `AIC vs v2.1` = sprintf("%+.0f", aic - aic[spec == "v2"]),
                     `Correlation of effects` = sprintf("%.2f", r_v2)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

- **Without absence** the effect falls from `r pc(t_at("v2", "effect"))`
  to `r pc(t_at("no_absence", "effect"))`, indistinguishable from zero.
- **Without neighbourhood education** or **without prior attainment** it
  grows, to `r pc(t_at("no_l4", "effect"))` and
  `r pc(t_at("no_ks2", "effect"))`. Both are already working: the city's
  intakes are more advantaged on both, and the model credits that. See
  [neighbourhood education](#sec-neighbourhood) below.
- **Local segregation** changes nothing. `r LA`'s catchment admissions,
  with random allocation as a tie-break, keep its schools relatively mixed, but that does not explain the effect.
- **The 11–16 flag**, added in v2.1, takes a little off: without it, as
  in v2.0, the effect is `r pc(t_at("age16", "effect"))`.
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * c_at(LA, "age16"))` of `r LA`'s school-years
  are at 11–16 schools, against
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * c_at("England", "age16"))` in England, and
  nationally 11–16 schools score `r pc(B$coefs[["age16"]])` higher.

**The arithmetic.** Over 2021/22 to 2024/25, the four years the model is
fitted on, `r LA`'s schools average `r sprintf("%.1f%%", c_at(LA, "total"))`
full-year absence against `r sprintf("%.1f%%", c_at("England", "total"))`
for England (means of school-years),
`r ord(B$ranks[["absence"]])` highest of `r B$ranks[["n_la"]]` authorities.
In `r abs_yr` alone, the year the
[area page's add-and-take figure](areas/brighton_and_hove.qmd#add-take)
uses, it was `r sprintf("%.1f%%", lat_la)` against
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", lat_eng)` (means of schools): the gap has
`r ifelse(lat_la - lat_eng > gap("total"), "widened", "narrowed")`.
On the v2.1 absence coefficient (`r sprintf("%.3f", B$coefs[["absence"]])`,
an elasticity), that difference lowers expected Attainment 8 by
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * B$cost)`. The authority effect, `r pc(t_at("v2", "effect"))`, almost
exactly gives it back. `r LA`'s schools attain about what similar intakes
attain elsewhere. They do it despite absence that, elsewhere, goes with
lower results.

Inside the city, absence costs about what it costs elsewhere. A school with
more absence than its neighbours does worse by about the national rate:
the interaction is `r sprintf("%+.3f", B$slope[2, 1])` (standard error
`r sprintf("%.3f", B$slope[2, 2])`). It is the city's *level* of absence
that carries no penalty, not its slope.

# What kind of absence

```{r tbl-comp}
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0("Absence in ", LA, " and England, % of possible sessions, mean of school-years 2021/22 to 2024/25 (DfE school absence data).")
tibble(Measure = c("All absence", "Illness (authorised)", "Unauthorised", "Other authorised", "Illness share of absence"),
       a = c(c_at(LA, "total"), c_at(LA, "illness"), c_at(LA, "unauthorised"), c_at(LA, "auth_other"), c_at(LA, "ill_share")),
       e = c(c_at("England", "total"), c_at("England", "illness"), c_at("England", "unauthorised"), c_at("England", "auth_other"), c_at("England", "ill_share"))) |>
  transmute(Measure, !!LA := sprintf("%.1f", a), England = sprintf("%.1f", e), Difference = sprintf("%+.1f", a - e)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrr")
```

Of `r LA`'s `r sprintf("%.1f", gap("total"))` points of extra absence,
`r sprintf("%.1f", gap("illness"))` is authorised illness. Unauthorised
absence is close to England's. Illness makes up
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", c_at(LA, "ill_share"))` of absence in the city
(`r ord(B$ranks[["ill_share"]])` highest share of `r B$ranks[["n_la"]]`).

Nationally, illness absence costs less than other absence. Split in two, a
1% rise in illness absence goes with `r pc(B$coefs[["illness"]] / 100, 2)`
Attainment 8 and a 1% rise in other absence with
`r pc(B$coefs[["other"]] / 100, 2)`. Allowing for that takes some of the
effect away: to `r pc(t_at("ill_share", "effect"))` with the illness
share, `r pc(t_at("split", "effect"))` with absence split. It does not
take most of it away. Absence's *type*, as DfE records it, is part of the
story, not the whole of it.

# Neighbourhood education {#sec-neighbourhood}

```{r neigh-setup}
#| include: false
N <- B$neigh; NP <- B$neigh_place
n_at <- function(s, col) N[[col]][N$spec == s]
la_urns <- V$schools$URN[V$schools$LANAME == LA]
dec <- decompose(V, la_urns, LA, groups = c("all", "disadvantaged", "non_disadvantaged"))
d_at <- function(g, comp) dec$points[dec$group == GROUP_LABELS[[g]] & dec$component == comp]
z_coef <- function(g) exp(V$coefs$estimate[V$coefs$group == g & V$coefs$term == "z_l4"]) - 1   # as a percentage change, as the methodology reports it
absorbed <- 1 - n_at("k150", "effect") / n_at("none", "effect")
best <- N |> filter(spec != "none") |> slice_min(aic, n = 1)
sc <- NP$schools |> left_join(V$schools |> select(URN, SCHNAME), by = "URN") |> arrange(desc(l4))
```

v2.1 measures neighbourhood education as the share of adults with a
degree-level (level 4+) qualification in the 150 Census output areas
nearest each school, from the 2021 Census. It is there because a school's
results follow the education of the families around it, and FSM sees only
the bottom of that.

**Where the city's schools sit.** Their neighbourhoods average
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", NP$la_l4)` of adults at level 4+, against
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", NP$eng_l4)` around England's schools: about
`r zz <- (NP$la_l4 - NP$eng_l4) / NP$sd_l4; sprintf("%.1f standard deviation%s", zz, ifelse(round(zz, 1) == 1, "", "s"))`
higher, `r ord(NP$la_rank)` of `r NP$n_la` authorities. The share with no
qualifications is `r sprintf("%.1f%%", NP$la_noq)` against
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", NP$eng_noq)`.
`r k <- sum(sc$pct_england >= 0.5); if (k == nrow(sc)) "Every one of the city's schools sits above England's median school:" else sprintf("%d of the city's %d schools sit above England's median school:", k, nrow(sc))`

```{r tbl-neigh-schools}
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0(LA, "'s schools' neighbourhoods, 2021 Census. Level 4+ is the share of adults with a degree-level qualification; the percentile places each school among England's.")
sc |> transmute(School = SCHNAME, `Level 4+, 150 nearest` = sprintf("%.1f%%", l4),
                `Level 4+, 10 nearest` = sprintf("%.1f%%", l4_10),
                `No qualifications, 150 nearest` = sprintf("%.1f%%", noq),
                `Percentile in England` = sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pct_england)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

**What the model already credits.** Each standard deviation of
neighbourhood education is worth `r pc(z_coef("all"), 2)` of Attainment 8
for all pupils, `r pc(z_coef("non_disadvantaged"), 2)` for
non-disadvantaged pupils and only `r pc(z_coef("disadvantaged"), 2)` for
disadvantaged ones. Set against England, the city's neighbourhoods lift
its schools' expected Attainment 8 by about
`r sprintf("%+.1f", d_at("all", "Neighbourhood education"))` points for all
pupils, `r sprintf("%+.1f", d_at("non_disadvantaged", "Neighbourhood education"))`
for non-disadvantaged and
`r sprintf("%+.1f", d_at("disadvantaged", "Neighbourhood education"))` for
disadvantaged pupils. That is credit the schools do not get: it is in the
expectation, not in their value added.

Without the term, the authority effect would be
`r pc(n_at("none", "effect"))` (`r ord(n_at("none", "rank"))`) rather than
`r pc(n_at("k150", "effect"))`. Neighbourhood education already accounts
for about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * absorbed)` of what would otherwise
look like a city effect.

**Would a better measure take more?** The table refits the model with the
neighbourhood drawn at every scale the original project built, and with
the share of adults with no qualifications:

```{r tbl-neigh}
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0(LA, "'s authority effect, all pupils, with neighbourhood education measured in different ways. AIC is against v2.1 (lower is better). Fitted on every school-year with each measure, so the v2.1 row matches the published effect.")
N |> transmute(Measure = label, Effect = pc(effect), Rank = paste(rank, "of", n_la),
               `AIC vs v2.1` = sprintf("%+.0f", aic - aic[spec == "k150"])) |>
  kt(align = "lrrr")
```

No. A more local neighbourhood fits worse at every step, and leaves the
city's effect *larger*: `r pc(n_at("k5", "effect"))` with the 5 nearest
output areas. The no-qualifications share fits worse than level 4+. The
best fit, `r tolower(best$label)`, moves the effect only to
`r pc(best$effect)`. Neighbourhood education is doing what it can, and
the rest is not a neighbourhood the Census can see.

**What it cannot see.** The measure counts every adult, not parents.
`r LA` has two universities: students, whose highest qualification while
studying is usually level 3, and young graduates without school-age
children both sit in the count, in opposite directions, and neither says
much about the families whose children attend the schools. A measure of
parents' qualifications, from the Census tables for households with
dependent children, would test this directly (reading 1 below).

# So what is it?

The data are school-level, so they cannot settle this. Four readings fit
what is above, and they are not exclusive.

1. **Family resources that keep learning going.** A day off costs less when someone at home can help catch up:
   parents with degrees, flexible or home-based work, tutoring, books. FSM
   does not see this, and neither, quite, does neighbourhood education,
   which already takes about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * absorbed)` of the effect and can take no more
   however it is drawn ([above](#sec-neighbourhood)). It counts every
   adult, not parents.
   The effect is largest for boys and non-disadvantaged pupils (3rd of
   151–152 for both). It is also present for disadvantaged pupils (16th),
   which fits a city with many lower-income households that are highly
   educated.
2. **Absence as a stand-in.** Across England, high absence travels with
   things the model does not measure: family stress, poverty beyond FSM,
   disengagement. Part of the absence coefficient is those things, not
   the days missed. Where absence comes from somewhere else, the model
   over-predicts its cost. In `r LA` it is mostly authorised illness,
   which may include anxiety and other health-related absence that
   follows a different pattern from disengagement. On this reading the authority effect is partly an artefact of
   how v2.1 treats absence, not something the schools do.
3. **Recording.** Schools and authorities differ in when they authorise
   illness and how they code it. A practice that authorises more
   parent-reported illness raises recorded absence without changing
   learning. This would show up as exactly this pattern, and school-level
   data cannot tell it from reading 2.
4. **Something the schools or the system do.** The 11–16 structure, where
   entry to the city's sixth-form colleges depends on GCSE grades, explains
   a little. Mixed intakes explain nothing measurable. Whatever is left
   after absence (`r pc(t_at("no_absence", "effect"))`, ranked
   `r ord(t_at("no_absence", "rank"))`) is ordinary.

# What would help tell them apart

All of these are published:

- **Absence by pupil characteristics, by authority** (DfE, *Pupil absence
  in schools in England*). Is the city's extra absence among pupils
  eligible for free school meals or not, and in which year groups? Reading 1
  predicts it is mostly among the non-disadvantaged.
- **Census 2021 qualifications for parents rather than all adults**:
  households with dependent children by the household reference person's
  qualification or NS-SeC, for school neighbourhoods. This would test
  reading 1 directly, and would improve v2.1's neighbourhood term
  everywhere students and young graduates are concentrated.
- **Persistent absence and absence reasons by authority over time**, against
  attainment. Reading 3 predicts the city's illness authorisation sits apart
  from its neighbours' with no matching change in attainment.
- **Elective home education and children missing education** (DfE, by
  authority). These show whether pupils leave school rolls before Year 11
  at unusual rates, which would change who sits GCSEs.
- **Attainment by prior-attainment band** in the KS4 performance tables:
  whether the effect sits with high, middle or low prior attainers.

# What it means for v2.1

v2.1 took the 11–16 flag into the expectation: it is a school's
structure, like its admissions policy. It treats a day of absence the
same whatever its cause. Adding the illness share of absence improves the
fit (AIC `r sprintf("%+.0f", t_at("ill_share", "aic") - t_at("v2", "aic"))`)
and barely changes other authorities' effects (correlation
`r sprintf("%.3f", t_at("ill_share", "r_v2"))`), but whether an absence is
authorised as illness is partly the school's own coding, so it stays out
of the headline. Value added allowing for the kind of absence is
published beside it instead ([the methodology](method.qmd#sec-v21)).
Neither removes `r LA`'s effect. Until the questions above are answered, read the
city's authority effect this way: its schools achieve as much as similar
schools elsewhere despite unusually high, mostly illness, absence. It is
not evidence that the city's schools add more than others. With
[no allowance for absence](method.qmd#sec-no-allowance), the city's
schools average `r sgn(m2_la$va)` points of value added,
`r ord(m2_la$rank)` of `r nrow(m2)` authorities.

The models are in `R/06_bh_effect.R`.
